chapters.title: Chapter 22: Turing’s Machine

passages.chapter-22-p-dad3b60500: After Gödel, Hilbert and Ackermann’s decision problem remained open. Remember the distinction: checking a proof already in your hands differs from giving a formula to a machine and demanding that it always return a decision about validity. We could know that certain theories were incomplete and still ask for a general decision procedure for first-order logic.
passages.chapter-22-p-0f895c55a7: But what counted as a procedure? Leave the word open and every claim of impossibility can meet the same reply: perhaps you have simply not thought of the right method. Before closing the door, you need to make mechanical calculation precise. Turing took hold of the question there.
passages.chapter-22-p-d4c9a749c0: In Cambridge, the mathematician Max Newman taught a course on the foundations of mathematics. He explained Gödel’s result and mentioned a question still open: could a mechanical procedure decide whether an arbitrary formula of first-order logic was logically valid?
passages.chapter-22-p-a730f78c2e: In the audience was a twenty-two-year-old named Alan Turing.
passages.chapter-22-p-e3e250d8c6: In 1936, Turing published “On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem.” To answer the decision problem, he had to give precise form to a more basic question: what does computation mean?
passages.chapter-22-p-a97a9e9bf1: The familiar account places the main idea in Grantchester meadows, near Cambridge, in the summer of 1935. Turing imagined a human calculator following rules and writing symbols on paper. What made that process mechanical?
passages.chapter-22-p-c6cc92212d: His answer stripped away what was inessential. A tape divided into squares, each containing a symbol. A head that reads its square, writes a symbol, and moves one square left or right. A finite collection of internal states. A rule table specifying what to do for a combination of state and scanned symbol.
passages.chapter-22-p-bd6543175e: Tape, head, states, rules. A Turing machine.
passages.chapter-22-p-32cef3c79a: Operate one yourself. Represent three by three consecutive marks, 111, and start the head on the first mark. The task is to add one. If the machine reads 1, it leaves the mark and moves right. If it reads a blank, it writes 1 and enters a halt state. It passes the three marks, writes in the fourth square, and stops. The result is 1111.
passages.chapter-22-p-650be9a9e0: The machine did not need to understand “three” or notice that it was adding. We chose the representation; it executed transitions. For multiplication or a primality test, the rule table becomes larger and additional states and symbols keep track of progress. The permitted elementary operations remain the same. The abstraction lets the task grow without introducing a new kind of magic inside the machine.
passages.chapter-22-p-44e12929c5: Its simplicity was the point. You could simulate it with paper and patience. The claim that this model captures every effective mechanical procedure is what we now call the Church–Turing thesis. Equivalences among formal models can be proved; identifying them with the informal idea of every effective procedure also involves explaining why that idea has been captured. The thesis is not a claim that every precisely stated question has an answer a machine can compute.
passages.chapter-22-p-858a3248f4: Turing then showed that some questions about these machines admit no general decider. In the familiar modern presentation, no program always correctly decides whether any supplied program and input will halt. His original paper used questions about machines continuing to produce symbols and connected them to the decision problem. Particular cases can be easy. The impossible request is a correct, terminating answer for every case.

It asks the checker what happens when a supplied program receives its own description. If the checker predicts a halt, the contrary program loops forever. If it predicts an endless run, the contrary program halts.

If the checker predicts that it continues, its instruction makes it stop. Either prediction is wrong. We did not hide a shortage of memory or demand an answer too quickly. We constructed a case inside the checker’s own promise that the promise cannot cover.
passages.chapter-22-p-a28da9e32a: The self-reference has returned in program form. A program can receive a program description, and the checker claiming to cover everything finds itself inside the demand. We can decide many cases, including the incrementer we just operated. The word that failed was “every.”
passages.chapter-22-p-77408d133e: The London Mathematical Society received the paper on 28 May 1936; it was read on 12 November. Its eventual importance was far greater than its immediate audience.

On an empty input, the very first rule application writes one mark and halts. We do not need a special exception for zero.
passages.chapter-22-p-a744a706e2: The program, current state, head position, and tape contents are different things. The same program accepts different inputs. The state tells us which stage of the procedure we are in. The tape carries the changing data. To describe the complete configuration at an instant, we need the state, head position, and tape—not merely the symbol currently under the head.
passages.chapter-22-p-5cefc989d0: This example uses a stay-put move for convenience. Such a move can be simulated by extra left/right moves and states; it does not add a new kind of computability. The ten visible squares also belong to our interface, not to Turing’s abstract definition. The formal machine can use as much tape as a finite computation requires.
passages.chapter-22-p-f6197755eb: Now choose the oscillating program. One state moves right; the other moves left. Neither rule enters a halt state. We can prove that this machine does not halt by examining the rule table. Merely watching an unfamiliar machine for forty steps and seeing no halt would be weaker evidence. Forty-one might have been the step that finished it.
passages.chapter-22-p-04f3047380: The distinction will matter: proving that a particular program stops, proving that another does not, and demanding one always-correct procedure for every possible program are three different requests.
passages.chapter-22-p-d5397f8a4c: Alonzo Church at Princeton had independently obtained the negative answer using a different formalism, lambda calculus. Turing’s result was not first, but his machine supplied an unusually concrete account of effective calculation. Turing went to Princeton to study with Church. The two approaches did not leave us competing kinds of computability: their equivalence became part of the story.
passages.chapter-22-p-7b1e25d25a: The negative answer to the decision problem now came with a positive description of calculation. Inside the paper was a machine stranger than an adder or divider: a machine that reads the description of another machine and runs it.

chapters.title: Chapter 23: The Universal Machine

passages.chapter-23-p-3cbe0776b3: Alongside its negative result, Turing's paper contained a positive idea that would change the world: a universal Turing machine.
passages.chapter-23-p-3e261e8d31: Most Turing machines are special-purpose — one adds, another multiplies, another checks if a number is prime.
passages.chapter-23-p-6d86d82510: But Turing showed you could build a machine that simulates any other Turing machine. Feed it a description of machine M and an input I. It pretends to be M, processes I, produces whatever M would produce. One machine, all computations.
passages.chapter-23-p-1ff959ea74: The move that makes this work is the move that makes all of modern computing work: the description of which Turing machine to simulate is itself written as data on the tape. The universal machine reads that description the same way it reads any other input — symbol by symbol, following its fixed table of rules — and from those symbols it works out how the simulated machine would behave at each step. The program is not built into the hardware. It is information, stored alongside the data the program operates on, and read by the same head that reads everything else.
passages.chapter-23-p-412af8ec6a: Before Turing, a calculating machine was a calculating machine; a loom that wove a particular pattern wove that pattern; a Jacquard card encoded one design at a time. The physical device and the task it performed were a single object. Turing's universal machine separated them. The same physical device, given different symbols on its tape, becomes a different machine: a calculator, a compiler, a game, a simulator of any other Turing machine, including a simulator of itself simulating something else.
passages.chapter-23-p-9142110cbe: This is the theoretical foundation of the programmable computer. The hardware stays fixed; the software — the description of which machine to simulate — changes. Load one program and it's a calculator; load another and it's a game, or a compiler.
passages.chapter-23-p-73f98b08a1: The idea would take a decade to become engineering. The first electronic computers of the early 1940s — Colossus at Bletchley, ENIAC at the Moore School — were not stored-program machines in Turing's sense. They were rewired for each new problem. Switching ENIAC from one ballistic calculation to another meant physically reconfiguring cables and switches; a job that could take days. The machine was universal in principle, in the way any sufficiently flexible calculator is, but its program lived in its wiring rather than its memory. It was a Turing machine whose tape contained data but not the description of itself.
passages.chapter-23-p-2764479f23: In 1945, John von Neumann wrote the document that fixed this: the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. EDVAC was the planned successor to ENIAC, and von Neumann's report — circulated among the engineers building it — set out a structure in which instructions and data shared the same memory, both encoded as numbers, both fetched and acted on by the same central unit. Whether a particular pattern of bits counted as program or as data was a question about how those bits were being used at a given moment, not a question about where they lived. Every computer built since has been a version of this design, which is why it is now called the von Neumann architecture even though Turing's 1936 paper had already shown why it had to exist.
passages.chapter-23-p-0a2de12f39: A universal machine receives two descriptions: a program PPP and its input xxx. It interprets the program’s rules and reproduces its steps. In modern notation, U(P,x)U(P,x)U(P,x) behaves like running PPP on xxx. If that run never finishes, the simulation is not obliged to finish either.
passages.chapter-23-p-98e612c239: The important change is where the rules live. In the small incrementer, we treated them as a fixed table. In the universal construction, a description of another machine can itself be input data. A single interpreter can therefore carry out many procedures without being rebuilt for each one. This is a claim about simulation, not a promise of unlimited speed, memory, or truth.
passages.chapter-23-p-b75e15bc20: To see the limit, suppose we have a total algorithm H(P,x)H(P,x)H(P,x) that always stops and correctly reports whether PPP stops on xxx. Build a program DDD using it:
passages.chapter-23-p-da301733ed: Feed DDD its own program description. If H(D,D)H(D,D)H(D,D) says “halts,” the definition of DDD makes it loop. If H(D,D)H(D,D)H(D,D) says “does not halt,” the definition makes it halt. Either answer is wrong. The assumed universally correct, always-terminating decider cannot exist.
passages.chapter-23-p-50836d5350: Nothing in this argument forbids useful termination checkers. A checker may handle a restricted language, prove termination of some programs, or answer “unknown” on difficult cases. A tool that sometimes says “unknown” has not contradicted the theorem because it never promised the impossible combination of universality, correctness, and a yes/no answer every time.
passages.chapter-23-p-6dac9f602d: This is the modern halting-problem presentation. Turing’s 1936 paper used related questions about machines producing symbols and connected undecidability to the decision problem for first-order logic. Calling the two presentations identical would erase a historical distinction. And first-order validity is not the same question as the truth of every sentence about the standard natural numbers.
passages.chapter-23-p-4b7e6621d8: The practical lesson survives those distinctions: a program can be described precisely enough to execute without there being one algorithm that settles every global question we might ask about its behaviour.
passages.chapter-23-p-2c48fb050d: Turing was 24 years old. He'd proven the most ambitious form of the foundational dream was impossible, and in the same paper invented the theoretical basis for the most powerful technology humanity would ever build.
passages.chapter-23-p-0e2ffd1cb7: Out of the failure of the dream came the machine.

chapters.title: Chapter 24: Convergence

passages.chapter-24-p-fb06b80674: Turing wasn't alone. Alonzo Church at Princeton developed lambda calculus — a different formalism — and independently proved the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable. In Warsaw, Emil Post described machines almost identical to Turing's. Stephen Kleene, working with Church, formalised a third route through what he called recursive functions: a class of arithmetical procedures built up from a handful of base operations. Several approaches, same result. And every definition of "computable" the participants compared turned out to be equivalent.
passages.chapter-24-p-3b57e2fbc6: Lambda calculus is worth pausing on, because it looks so unlike Turing's tape-and-head device that the equivalence comes as a shock. Church's primitive object is not a machine but an expression. The single operation is function application: given a function f and an argument x, evaluate f(x). Functions can take functions as arguments and return functions as values. There is no memory, no read head, no clock — only expressions being rewritten by substitution. From this minimal grammar, Church showed how to encode numbers, booleans, arithmetic, conditionals, recursion, every construct a programmer recognises. The lambda calculus is the ancestor of LISP, of Haskell, of the functional features that have crept into every modern language.
passages.chapter-24-p-6aa12876fe: Turing then proved what Church had been unable to prove alone: that any function the lambda calculus can compute, a Turing machine can compute, and vice versa. A tape-shuffling automaton and a rewriting-rule grammar, with no shared vocabulary, define the same class of functions. Post's production systems, working from yet another starting point — strings rewritten by formal rules — fit the same boundary. Kleene's recursive functions, defined arithmetically, fit it too.
passages.chapter-24-p-1b42234a3d: When formalisms invented in different countries, with different aesthetics, in pursuit of different questions, converge on exactly the same class of computable functions, the boundary they are tracing is probably real. It is not an artefact of any one notation. It is a feature of what computation is. The Church-Turing thesis, as it became known, says that this shared boundary is the boundary of effective calculability as such — that any procedure a human can follow by rote, with paper and pencil and enough patience, falls inside it.
passages.chapter-24-p-983d0c03a2: The thesis is still unproven and might be unprovable; it is a claim about an informal notion ("what a human could in principle compute") matching a formal one. But no one has ever found a counterexample. Every computational system we've built can be simulated by a Turing machine. The universality was discovered, not designed.

chapters.title: Chapter 25: Shannon

passages.chapter-25-p-5d9b9b8c00: Claude Elwood Shannon was born in Petoskey, Michigan, in 1916, the son of a probate judge and a high-school principal. He grew up taking things apart. As a boy he ran a telegraph line of his own design between his house and a friend's farm, half a mile away, using barbed wire as the transmission medium. The barbed wire worked. It carried Morse code along a fence that was meant to keep cattle in.
passages.chapter-25-p-48185fc765: He arrived at MIT in 1936 as a master's student, and within a year wrote a thesis called A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits. The argument fit on seventy-two pages. An electrical relay is open or closed; a Boolean variable is true or false; the algebra George Boole had laid out in 1854 to formalize "the laws of thought" was, in its formal structure, the same algebra you needed to design any circuit built out of relays. Series wiring computes AND. Parallel wiring computes OR. A relay that opens when energized computes NOT. Any logical function whatsoever could therefore be built from a finite arrangement of switches, and conversely, any circuit could be analyzed by reducing it to a Boolean expression and simplifying it the way an algebraist simplifies an equation. Howard Gardner later called it the most important master's thesis of the century. The judgment is hard to argue with — every digital chip ever fabricated is a physical realization of what Shannon wrote down at twenty-one.
passages.chapter-25-p-1e63d138ce: The structural point is the one that matters for this book. Before Shannon, the logical tradition and the engineering tradition spoke different languages. Boole's algebra lived in philosophy journals. Relay circuits lived in telephone-exchange manuals. The thesis proved that the two vocabularies described the same object. A philosopher in 1854 trying to formalize reasoning, and a Bell engineer in 1937 trying to route calls without crossed wires, had been doing the same mathematics. Boole had died in 1864, walking through the rain to give a lecture, never having seen an electric light or imagined an electronic circuit. His algebra had sat in journals for eighty years before Shannon connected it to copper.
passages.chapter-25-p-23d085f873: Eleven years later, working at Bell Labs, Shannon did it again from the other side. A Mathematical Theory of Communication, published in the Bell System Technical Journal in 1948, gave information a unit and a measure. The unit was the bit — a coinage Shannon credited to John Tukey. The measure was entropy, the average uncertainty in a source's output, computed by the same formula Boltzmann had used to count the microstates of a gas. A message is informative to the degree that it reduces uncertainty; a channel has a finite capacity for moving uncertainty from one end to the other; and Shannon's coding theorems specified, exactly, how close to that capacity you could get and how far you could compress a source before its entropy refused to compress further.
passages.chapter-25-p-349d0512a1: The naming was a joke that stuck. When Shannon asked John von Neumann what to call the new measure, von Neumann told him: "Call it entropy. In the first place, the formula is the same as Boltzmann's. In the second place, nobody really knows what entropy is, so in a debate you will always have the advantage." He was joking. He was also right — the formula was the same because both thermodynamics and communication describe systems exploring state spaces under constraints. The math of equilibrium and the math of optimal coding are the same math.
passages.chapter-25-p-cce1486f33: The 1937 thesis had married Boole's logic to electrical hardware. The 1948 paper married Boltzmann's statistics to communication. Shannon was the only person who did both, and the two papers together explain why this book has two threads. Logic and optimization, symbol and probability, the discrete and the statistical — they meet in his work and nowhere else so cleanly. Every transformer trained today minimizes a cross-entropy loss that Shannon defined, running on logic gates whose design rules Shannon proved correct.

passages.chapter-25-p-81309c0879: The biographical detail is harder to fit into a sentence. He juggled while riding a unicycle down the corridors of Bell Labs. He built a mechanical mouse named Theseus that learned to solve a maze and remembered the solution on subsequent runs — arguably the first machine-learning demonstration anyone had built. He kept a workshop full of gadgets at his house in Massachusetts: a chess-playing automaton, a flame-throwing trumpet, a machine whose only function was to extend a mechanical hand from a closed box and switch itself off. He was, by every account, a happy man.
passages.chapter-25-p-973a4cfb67: He published less and less after the 1950s. The work was done.

chapters.title: Chapter 26: The Logical Neuron

passages.chapter-26-p-5024669589: Walter Pitts was a fifteen-year-old runaway from Detroit who had taught himself logic by reading Bertrand Russell's Principia Mathematica — at age twelve. When Russell came to lecture at the University of Chicago in 1938, Pitts simply showed up and started attending classes. He had no money, no credentials, and nowhere to live; he slept in parks. But he understood Russell's logic better than most professors.
passages.chapter-26-p-ba12ac4dcd: Pitts caught the attention of Rudolf Carnap, one of the world's leading figures in symbolic logic. For years, Pitts haunted the University of Chicago — homeless, penniless, brilliant.
passages.chapter-26-p-1c608ba76a: In 1942, he met Warren McCulloch, a psychiatrist and neurophysiologist who was obsessed with a question: how does the brain compute? Their 1943 paper, "A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity," proposed that neurons could be modeled as logical gates. A neuron receives inputs, sums them with weights, and fires if the total exceeds a threshold. With the right connections, networks of such neurons could compute any logical function.
passages.chapter-26-p-390285ba20: The paper was dense with Russell-Whitehead notation — the very logic Pitts had taught himself as a child. It showed that neural networks could implement any proposition expressible in symbolic logic. And it suggested something more: that the brain itself might be a kind of computing machine, running software written in the language of formal logic.

passages.chapter-26-p-1b264e3072: John von Neumann cited the paper as foundational. It became one of the seeds of both artificial intelligence and cognitive science. The idea that intelligence might be computation, running on neural hardware, began here — in the collaboration between Pitts and McCulloch, built on the philosophical foundations of Russell's Principia.
passages.chapter-26-p-659634a1e3: Three philosophical traditions converged in a single decade. Boole's logic became Shannon's circuits; Russell's formal language supplied the notation for the McCulloch-Pitts neuron; and Turing's abstract machine was now the blueprint for the stored-program computer.

chapters.title: Chapter 27: The War

passages.chapter-27-p-e955495e7e: On September 4, 1939, the day after Britain declared war on Germany, Alan Turing reported for work at a Victorian mansion fifty miles north of London. Bletchley Park had been purchased the year before by the Government Code and Cypher School, which needed a safer home than London for what they knew was coming.
passages.chapter-27-p-42115b4e95: Nazi Germany encrypted its military communications using the Enigma machine — a device resembling an overgrown typewriter with a plugboard and multiple rotating cylinders. Each day, operators across the German military set their machines to new configurations. The number of possible settings was astronomical: over 103 sextillion combinations. Breaking the code by brute force was mathematically hopeless.
passages.chapter-27-p-c70308da96: Hilbert's program had declared a class of problems formally undecidable, and Turing himself had sharpened the verdict in 1936: certain questions admit no general mechanical procedure at all. Enigma traffic was protected by something close to that vocabulary — a key space so large that no algorithm of any conceivable description could search it. Yet Bletchley decoded the messages anyway, day after day, by attacking the small structural mistakes German operators made and the small leakages the machine's design allowed. The gap between "theoretically out of reach" and "tractable in practice" turned out to be a place a working engineer could live.
passages.chapter-27-p-5afa7d5735: The Polish Cipher Bureau had cracked earlier versions of Enigma in the 1930s, building a device called the "bomba" to automate part of the process. But by 1939, the Germans had added complexity faster than the Poles could keep up. Just before the invasion of Poland, Polish cryptographers handed their methods and their secrets to the British and French.
passages.chapter-27-p-d81edf694d: Turing was assigned to Hut 8, responsible for naval Enigma — the most difficult variant and the most important. Within months, he had designed the Bombe: a giant special-purpose search engine exploiting weaknesses in how German operators used Enigma. By 1943, over 200 Bombes were running. At its peak, Bletchley was cracking 84,000 Enigma messages per month.
passages.chapter-27-p-e1ede40156: The machines multiplied. Tommy Flowers built Colossus — an all-electronic machine using 2,400 vacuum tubes — to crack an even more complex German cipher. It was operational five days before D-Day. Across the Atlantic, ENIAC used 18,000 vacuum tubes for artillery calculations.
passages.chapter-27-p-a21111f154: By the time the war ended, the abstractions of 1936 — Turing's imaginary machines, Church's lambda calculus — had become iron and glass and electricity.
passages.chapter-27-p-3558c4b9c7: Bletchley's work remained classified for thirty years. The computer age had begun in a Victorian mansion, in wooden huts, among people who could never speak of what they'd done.

chapters.title: Chapter 28: The Architecture

passages.chapter-28-p-290cb62853: John von Neumann read Turing's 1936 paper. He understood immediately.
passages.chapter-28-p-7a66d26df8: Von Neumann was perhaps the most versatile genius of the twentieth century. Born into a wealthy Jewish family in Budapest in 1903, he showed signs of prodigy from childhood — by age six he could divide eight-digit numbers in his head; by eight he had absorbed calculus. He published his first mathematical paper at eighteen. By the time he was thirty, he had made foundational contributions to set theory, quantum mechanics, and mathematical economics.
passages.chapter-28-p-b106ae4c18: In August 1944, von Neumann was waiting for a train at Aberdeen, Maryland, when he fell into conversation with Herman Goldstine, an Army officer working on the ENIAC project. Within weeks, von Neumann was consulting on both ENIAC and its planned successor, EDVAC. He immediately grasped the problem: ENIAC was "programmed" by physically rewiring panels. Changing what it computed meant rebuilding part of the machine.
passages.chapter-28-p-ca648cb635: The EDVAC team — principally J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly — had already conceived a solution: store the program in electronic memory, just like the data. The hardware would become general.
passages.chapter-28-p-da5da28332: This was Turing's universal machine made practical.
passages.chapter-28-p-b9236acdb9: In the spring of 1945, he produced "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" — 101 pages that would become the most influential document in computing history. It described the "von Neumann architecture": a central processing unit, a memory that holds both program and data, and input/output systems.
passages.chapter-28-p-982b43d128: This is still how your computer works — and your phone, and every server, laptop, and game console.
passages.chapter-28-p-53b25da758: Between the theoretical foundations and the dream of artificial intelligence lay fifty years of engineering. Sorting, searching, graph traversal, dynamic programming, data structures — the toolkit of computer science, the practical art of making machines do useful work efficiently. Donald Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming, begun in 1962 and still unfinished, is the monument of this era. This work is invisible in histories of ideas because it looks like engineering rather than philosophy. But it built the infrastructure everything else runs on.

chapters.title: Chapter 29: Cybernetics

passages.chapter-29-p-9b59001448: Before the AI pioneers named their field, another group had already staked a claim on the territory.
passages.chapter-29-p-c89b8dcdb5: In 1948, Norbert Wiener published Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine. The title was a program. Wiener argued that the same mathematical principles governed communication and control in living organisms and in machines. Feedback loops — systems that measure their own output and adjust — were the common architecture. A thermostat, a reflex arc, an anti-aircraft gun tracking a plane, a human reaching for a cup of coffee: all were systems using feedback to minimize error.
passages.chapter-29-p-eefab12029: The word "cybernetics" came from the Greek kybernetes, meaning steersman or governor. Wiener chose it deliberately. The core insight was about steering: how systems maintain themselves, correct themselves, pursue goals through continuous adjustment.
passages.chapter-29-p-6aba122e20: A feedback loop is a system that measures the difference between where it is and where it wants to be — the error — and adjusts in the direction that reduces the error. Wiener didn't use the language of optimization, but the structure is identical: the thermostat follows the gradient toward the set temperature, and the anti-aircraft gun follows the gradient toward the target.
passages.chapter-29-p-58d1578752: Wiener's circle overlapped with the neural network pioneers. McCulloch and Pitts were cybernetics insiders. So was John von Neumann. The Macy Conferences on cybernetics (1946–1953) brought together neurophysiologists, mathematicians, engineers, and social scientists in a sustained conversation about feedback, information, and self-organizing systems.
passages.chapter-29-p-6de3e8d45c: But cybernetics also carried a warning. Wiener was deeply concerned about what happened when feedback systems interacted with human society. His 1950 book The Human Use of Human Beings argued that automated systems could concentrate power in ways their designers didn't intend. He was thinking about alignment before the word existed. The field ignored him for seventy years and then reinvented his concerns from scratch.
passages.chapter-29-p-03e18a8fcb: Consider a deliberately simple controller. A quantity xxx should reach 10. At each step, measure the gap and correct a fraction kkk of it:
passages.chapter-29-p-f0bc7adf30: Start at zero with k=0.5k=0.5k=0.5. The values are 0,5,7.5,8.75,9.3750,5,7.5,8.75,9.3750,5,7.5,8.75,9.375. Each step halves the remaining error. We do not need the controller to know a complete plan in advance; it keeps asking how far the result is from the target.
passages.chapter-29-p-c07710e5ed: But “correct more strongly” is not a universal improvement. At k=1.5k=1.5k=1.5, the sequence begins 0,15,7.5,11.25,9.3750,15,7.5,11.25,9.3750,15,7.5,11.25,9.375. It crosses the target repeatedly while the oscillation shrinks. At k=2k=2k=2, it bounces forever between 0 and 20. At k=2.1k=2.1k=2.1, the oscillation grows.
passages.chapter-29-p-f59ed40e85: Write the error as et=10−xte_t=10-x_tet​=10−xt​. The update becomes et+1=(1−k)ete_{t+1}=(1-k)e_tet+1​=(1−k)et​. Convergence requires ∣1−k∣<1|1-k|<1∣1−k∣<1, hence 0<k<20<k<20<k<2. We have a precise condition for this model, not a general slogan about the virtue of feedback.

The first values become 0,5,10,15,20,22.50,5,10,15,20,22.50,5,10,15,20,22.5. Even after reaching the target, the controller keeps correcting an old shortage. The no-delay stability condition is no longer sufficient.
passages.chapter-29-p-04c8ac0817: This is why a correction loop must be understood as a system: action size, measurement, delay, and the process being changed all matter. Our idealized quantity has no physical saturation or friction; it makes the mechanism visible by leaving those complications out.
passages.chapter-29-p-7fa3b1a54c: One question remains outside the recurrence. Why is the target 10? A controller can track the wrong target very well. Feedback helps connect action to measured consequence, but choosing the consequence that deserves attention is a further decision.
passages.chapter-29-p-25b744d12f: The cybernetics movement faded in the 1960s, absorbed partly into control theory, partly into computer science, partly into the new discipline that would claim the territory: artificial intelligence. But its core insight — that intelligent behavior emerges from feedback loops minimizing error rather than from logical deduction — would return with overwhelming force when neural networks finally worked.
passages.chapter-29-p-ab07866c82: It also returned in a quieter line. At MIT in the early 1980s, Rodney Brooks built robots without world models. His subsumption design used layers of reactive behaviours stacked on top of each other, with no central planner and no symbolic reasoning anywhere in the loop. The robots walked over rough ground while the symbolic-AI robots, equipped with detailed internal maps, fell over. Brooks did not call what he was doing a third mode, but the underlying move is recognisable: attend to what is actually there, not to what your theory says ought to be there.

chapters.title: Chapter 30: The Question of the Machine

passages.chapter-30-p-910fb0d35a: In 1950, Turing published "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." It begins with a sentence that still provokes: "I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'"
passages.chapter-30-p-a4fb4e6cbe: Instead of defining "think" (a hopeless task), he proposed the imitation game — later called the Turing test.
passages.chapter-30-p-370a7b854f: A human interrogator communicates by text with two hidden entities — one human, one machine. If the interrogator can't reliably distinguish them, the machine has passed. It has, in some operational sense, demonstrated thinking.
passages.chapter-30-p-4ce32d2548: The original question — can machines think? — is metaphysical in the worst sense: it depends on what you mean by "think," and every definition smuggles in the answer. Turing's substitution replaces an unanswerable question with one a careful experimenter could in principle settle. If a machine can sustain an extended conversation indistinguishable from a human's, the burden of proof shifts.
passages.chapter-30-p-48cb5c3ad9: Most of the 1950 paper is given over to anticipated objections, answered in turn. The Theological Objection: only beings with immortal souls can think, and God has given souls only to humans. (Turing notes that this argument restricts God's freedom, and that theology has bad form on questions of natural science.) The "Heads in the Sand" Objection: the consequences of thinking machines are too dreadful to contemplate, so let us hope they are impossible. The Mathematical Objection, drawn from Gödel and from Turing's own earlier work: there are statements no formal system can decide, so machines must be limited in ways minds are not. (Turing's reply is that humans are demonstrably limited too, and there is no reason to think a machine's limits will be felt at the same places as a human's.) The Argument from Consciousness, drawn from Lady Lovelace's 1843 note on Babbage's Analytical Engine: a machine can only do what we tell it to do; it cannot originate. (Turing points out that this also applies to a child, programmed by genetics and upbringing, and we do not normally deny that children think.) He answered nine such objections in all, with a patience that reads almost wearily seventy-five years later, because we are still working through the same list.
passages.chapter-30-p-943ded8a6b: The test has aged in a way Turing would have found instructive. Modern large language models pass weaker versions of the imitation game routinely — sustained conversations, with millions of casual interrogators, in which the human side is often the one that gives itself away. The philosophical question has not been answered; systems now exhibit the behaviour his test was meant to certify, and the certifying does not feel like settlement.
passages.chapter-30-p-97416cd500: He was gesturing toward something that would take decades to articulate: that "thinking" might not be a binary, and that the question itself might be confused.

chapters.title: Chapter 31: The Tragedy

passages.chapter-31-p-f317ad034b: Alan Turing should have been celebrated. He'd laid the theoretical foundations of computation. He'd helped win the war. He was building the future of computing at Manchester.
passages.chapter-31-p-aa79144ecc: In January 1952, Turing's house was burgled. He reported it to the police. During the investigation, he mentioned a man named Arnold Murray, whom he'd been seeing. With what his biographer Andrew Hodges calls "self-destructive naivety," Turing simply told them the truth.
passages.chapter-31-p-1939f1a9a6: The police stopped investigating the burglary and started investigating Turing.
passages.chapter-31-p-c9d79938b3: Homosexuality was illegal in Britain. Turing was convicted on March 31, 1952. The judge offered him a choice: prison or chemical castration through estrogen injections. Turing chose the hormones.
passages.chapter-31-p-05e1bbbf3c: The treatment lasted a year. The estrogen rendered him impotent, caused weight gain, and made him develop breasts. His security clearance was revoked. He could no longer work on codes. MI5 began surveillance.
passages.chapter-31-p-0cbe95b45f: To his friends, Turing dealt with it "with as much humor and defiance as you could muster."
passages.chapter-31-p-b1723fbb52: On the morning of June 8, 1954, Turing's housekeeper found his body. He was lying in bed. A half-eaten apple lay beside him. He had died the previous day from cyanide poisoning.
passages.chapter-31-p-60cef9bf4c: The coroner ruled suicide. The apple was never tested for cyanide. Turing's mother refused to accept the verdict. Some biographers have speculated he was re-enacting a scene from Snow White, his favorite film — the poisoned apple, the eternal sleep.
passages.chapter-31-p-e61d87d818: Britain apologized in 2009. The Queen granted a posthumous pardon in 2013 — sixty years too late.
passages.chapter-31-p-fe7414287b: The founder of computer science, the war hero, the man who imagined artificial intelligence — destroyed by the country he had saved.

chapters.title: Chapter 32: Philosophy Becomes Software

passages.chapter-32-p-91d1d1dbea: Shannon showed that Boolean logic is circuit design.
passages.chapter-32-p-a1bc90d51a: Programming languages are philosophies made executable.
passages.chapter-32-p-66a526dd1a: In the late 1950s, John McCarthy at MIT created LISP — a programming language built directly on Alonzo Church's lambda calculus. LISP isn't inspired by lambda calculus, or loosely based on it; it is lambda calculus with a syntax. Church's theoretical formalism for defining computable functions, the one Turing had shown equivalent to his machines, became a language you could type into a computer. Functions as first-class objects, recursion as the primary control structure, symbolic expressions as data — all of it descended directly from Church's 1936 paper. When a programmer writes a LISP function, she is writing in a notation that Church invented to prove the Entscheidungsproblem unsolvable.
passages.chapter-32-p-9e60306337: A decade later, Alain Colmerauer and Robert Kowalski created Prolog — a language built on Frege's predicate logic. A Prolog program is a set of logical assertions and rules. Execution is inference: the system searches for proofs of your queries using resolution, a theorem-proving technique. When a programmer writes a Prolog rule, she is writing in the language Frege invented in Begriffsschrift. The dream of reducing reasoning to mechanical symbol manipulation — the dream Russell and Whitehead spent a decade pursuing — runs every time someone executes a Prolog program.
passages.chapter-32-p-fb9b56351f: C, by contrast, descended from a completely different lineage — close to the machine, imperative, concerned with memory addresses and processor instructions. Where LISP and Prolog trust abstraction, C trusts the hardware.
passages.chapter-32-p-a7ba2727f8: And Chomsky's hierarchy runs through all of them. Every programming language must be parsed — its text must be analyzed into a structure the computer can execute. The grammars that define this parsing are formal grammars in exactly Chomsky's sense. Context-free grammars, the middle level of his hierarchy, turned out to be precisely what compiler designers needed. Backus-Naur Form, the standard notation for defining programming language syntax since the 1960s, is a context-free grammar. Every time a compiler parses a line of code, it's using the mathematical framework a linguist built to understand human language.
passages.chapter-32-p-f7b978b370: Chomsky's hierarchy mapped levels of formal grammar onto levels of computational power: regular grammars to finite automata, context-free grammars to pushdown automata, context-sensitive grammars to linear-bounded automata, and unrestricted grammars to Turing machines. Chomsky discovered this while studying linguistics; computer scientists discovered they needed it while building compilers. The convergence happened because the structural constraints were the same.
passages.chapter-32-p-532c165fa0: Each language embodies a bet about what computation is: LISP bets on function application, Prolog on logical inference, C on instruction execution. The fact that all three work — that all three are Turing-complete, capable of computing anything computable — confirms the Church-Turing thesis from yet another angle. But the fact that they feel different, that certain problems are natural in one and tortured in another, shows that the choice of philosophical framework isn't neutral.

chapters.title: Chapter 33: How to Solve It

passages.chapter-33-p-65ed6470dc: In a graduate seminar at the ETH Zürich, sometime around 1924, the Hungarian mathematician George Pólya stopped at a result and told the room that the theorem had never been proved and might be difficult. He was about to move on. Five minutes later a young man at the back raised his hand. Pólya invited him to the blackboard. The student wrote down the proof.
passages.chapter-33-p-5121f124c7: "After that," Pólya said, looking back on it decades later, "I was afraid of von Neumann."
passages.chapter-33-p-f09e2b412e: He was telling the story against himself, but it captures the figure of Pólya: the teacher who could see what a student like that was. He spent his career trying to write down what people like that did. Not the proofs they produced, but the moves that produced them.
passages.chapter-33-p-4ac8839716: Pólya was born in Budapest in 1887, the son of a lawyer who had converted from Judaism to Catholicism in the hope of an academic appointment that never came. He took his doctorate in Vienna and Göttingen, settled at the ETH in 1914, and after Hitler's rise crossed the Atlantic to Stanford in 1940. He worked on combinatorics, on random walks, on conformal mapping. He proved that a drunkard walking randomly on a two-dimensional grid will almost certainly return to where he started but a drunkard walking on a three-dimensional lattice almost certainly won't — a result that turned out to matter for everything from polymer physics to the design of Monte Carlo algorithms. He was a working mathematician of the first rank.
passages.chapter-33-p-9f5f2a35d7: In 1945, twenty-five years before retirement, he published a slim book aimed at high-school teachers. He called it How to Solve It.
passages.chapter-33-p-ade32370ce: The book argues, in plain language, that mathematical discovery is not deduction. Deduction is what you write down after the work is over. Before that, you guess. You try analogies. You work backward from the answer you wish you had. You look at a simpler version of the problem. You assume the result and see what it would let you conclude. You stare at a special case until a pattern emerges. Pólya catalogued these moves and named them. He called them heuristics — old word, Greek, meaning aids to discovery. The book ends with a dictionary of sixty-seven of them.
passages.chapter-33-p-d36997dbea: The argument is not that heuristics are infallible. They aren't. The argument is that they are how mathematicians actually work, and that the practice can be made explicit. How to Solve It has sold over a million copies. It has been continuously in print for eighty years. It is the closest thing the discipline has to an operating manual.
passages.chapter-33-p-1045d69ad3: In 1957, Allen Newell, J.C. Shaw, and Herbert Simon — working at RAND and Carnegie — produced a program they called the General Problem Solver. GPS read a problem statement in a symbolic representation, identified the gap between current state and goal, and applied a heuristic called means-ends analysis to close it. The heuristic was, almost verbatim, Pólya's. Simon cited Pólya in print; Newell referred to How to Solve It as foundational. Marvin Minsky, writing his 1961 "Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence," said that everyone in the field should know Pólya's work.
passages.chapter-33-p-42c2a9c2e5: GPS worked on toy problems. It proved theorems in propositional logic, solved the Tower of Hanoi, found chess combinations a few moves deep. For a moment in the late 1950s it seemed possible that intelligence could be reached by writing down enough heuristics in enough generality.
passages.chapter-33-p-b3d65431b5: The problems Pólya had been describing for human mathematicians lived inside a small, curated space. A human reading a textbook is shown three or four candidate moves at each step; the search is hand-pruned by the problem-setter. The computer cannot be hand-pruned. When you take a heuristic that works at human scale and ask it to operate on the full state space of a real problem — chess, theorem proving, route planning, protein folding — the branches multiply faster than any heuristic can prune them. A chess position has on the order of 30 legal moves; ten moves ahead is a tree with 3010≈6×101430^{10} \approx 6 \times 10^{14}3010≈6×1014 leaves. Means-ends analysis prunes intelligently but not exponentially intelligently. The tree wins.
passages.chapter-33-p-5066badb7c: Complexity theory, named in the 1970s, gave it a mathematical description: there is a class of problems for which no known algorithm runs in time that grows polynomially with the input. The number of operations explodes. Computers running heuristics fall behind real-world problems the way Achilles fell behind the tortoise — and the wall is not a temporary failure of cleverness. It is, on present evidence, a fact of the territory.
passages.chapter-33-p-8942d6b430: Pólya himself never claimed otherwise. He was teaching teenagers and graduate students how to find proofs, not how to solve combinatorial chess. But the AI program that built on him claimed otherwise, and the claim broke against the wall.
passages.chapter-33-p-4817020c32: The response was to give up on solving and start approximating.
passages.chapter-33-p-a6692285c9: In 1975 John Holland published the first systematic treatment of genetic algorithms — populations of candidate solutions evolving under a fitness function, the optimization tradition rewriting Darwin in source code. In 1983 Scott Kirkpatrick, Dan Gelatt, and Mario Vecchi published "Optimization by Simulated Annealing" in Science, importing the statistical mechanics of Boltzmann's gas atoms into the design of integrated circuits — accept some bad moves early to escape local minima, cool the system, settle into a near-optimal configuration. Tabu search, beam search, A*, ant colonies, particle swarms, Monte Carlo tree search — for thirty years, the engineering response to NP-hardness was a proliferation of clever ways to get good enough answers without ever guaranteeing the best one. The optimization tradition the book has been tracing turned out to be exactly what the complexity wall had made necessary.
passages.chapter-33-p-c9c47e6413: These methods cracked some of what Pólya's program could not. Chess fell to specialized search in 1997. Logistics, scheduling, very-large-scale integration — all became domains where engineers could ship working systems that produced answers no one would have called optimal but that nobody could improve on within a budget. The wall stood; the engineers learned to climb partway up it and call that progress.
passages.chapter-33-p-c84410db2a: What none of the approximation methods could do, until very recently, was learn the heuristic from data.
passages.chapter-33-p-c81ebae432: Pólya wrote his heuristics by hand. Newell and Simon coded them by hand. Genetic algorithms and simulated annealing assumed a fitness function written by hand. The bottleneck of every approach was the human who had to know enough about the problem to design the search. When deep learning matured in the 2010s, that bottleneck moved. A neural network trained on millions of positions could learn a value function that pruned a search tree more aggressively than any heuristic Pólya had named. AlphaGo, in 2016, combined Monte Carlo tree search with two neural networks — one that proposed moves and one that evaluated positions — and beat a world champion at a game whose state space had defeated every previous symbolic and approximate approach. AlphaFold, in 2020, did the same to protein folding. The neural network was not solving the problem; it was producing the heuristic that made the search tractable.
passages.chapter-33-p-8529f5b1f9: Pólya was right that heuristics matter. He was wrong about who could write them. He thought it was teachers. It turned out to be gradient descent.
passages.chapter-33-p-bc8dc75c12: The logic tradition gave us the formal description of what computation is, and the complexity theory that bounds it. The optimization tradition gave us gradient descent, the engineering response to those bounds, and the modern machinery — neural networks, reinforcement learning — that finally delivered what Pólya's program had promised eighty years before. The student who frightened Pólya by writing down a proof in five minutes would, twenty years later, design the architecture every modern computer still runs — the machine that, six decades after his death, would learn to do at scale what Pólya could not write down.

chapters.title: Chapter 34: Monte Carlo

passages.chapter-34-p-6a648b2074: In late April 1946, Stanislaw Ulam returned to Los Alamos. He had been away nine months — a viral encephalitis the previous summer had put him into a coma; the doctors had drilled a hole in his skull to relieve the pressure, and when he woke he wasn't sure whether his mind was the one he had gone in with. He played a great deal of solitaire while convalescing, partly to test himself. The game he played most often was Canfield, a variant in which the player wins about one hand in thirty.
passages.chapter-34-p-2f42ce5391: What were the actual odds of a Canfield deal coming out? The combinatorics were hopeless. With fifty-two cards and a layout that changed at every play, there was no closed-form answer. The combinatorial tree of possibilities was, in the technical sense, larger than the working life of any mathematician.
passages.chapter-34-p-fb24b43a2e: Ulam noticed something. He didn't need to enumerate the tree. He could just play a hundred hands and count.
passages.chapter-34-p-f14bf57383: He told von Neumann. They had known each other since the 1930s, two of the Hungarian-Jewish mathematicians who had ended up in America with their old Europe destroyed. Von Neumann was at Los Alamos working on the hydrogen-bomb calculations, where the problem of neutron diffusion in fissile material had been generating the same shape of impossibility: equations that could be written down and not solved. In March 1947 von Neumann wrote a memorandum proposing a statistical approach. Nicholas Metropolis, working alongside them, gave it a name. Ulam had often mentioned his uncle Michał, who, Metropolis later recalled, "just had to go to Monte Carlo" to gamble. They called the method Monte Carlo.
passages.chapter-34-p-c3d378b273: The move was: when you cannot solve a problem, simulate it. Build a random process whose statistics, in the long run, are the answer you want. Roll it forward many times. The answer falls out as an average.
passages.chapter-34-p-c4f6b356bd: The trick was older than the name. Boltzmann had used it in spirit in the 1870s — he computed thermodynamic properties of gases not by tracking every molecule but by averaging over an ensemble of possible configurations weighted by their energy. Statistical mechanics is Monte Carlo's older sibling; what Ulam and von Neumann did was turn the ensemble average into an algorithm a machine could run.
passages.chapter-34-p-3cf5e24147: In 1953, Metropolis, along with Marshall and Arianna Rosenbluth and Edward and Augusta Teller, published "Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines" in the Journal of Chemical Physics. The paper described a way to sample from a probability distribution you couldn't write down in closed form: construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the one you want, take a step in the chain, accept the step if it lowers the energy, accept with diminishing probability if it raises the energy. Run for long enough and the chain's history is a sample from the distribution. The method came to be called the Metropolis algorithm; it was the first of what would later be named Markov Chain Monte Carlo, or MCMC. In 1970 the statistician W. K. Hastings generalised it, and by the 1990s MCMC had become the workhorse of Bayesian inference. Computational physicists, biologists, economists, and machine-learning researchers all use the same move — when the integral is intractable, set up a chain that samples from it and take the average.
passages.chapter-34-p-da2c749035: This was, in a way, the optimization thread's other algorithm. Gradient descent followed the slope of a landscape downhill. Monte Carlo dropped pebbles at random and counted where they piled up. Where the gradient method assumed smoothness, the sampling method assumed nothing about the surface — only that you could evaluate it at points.
passages.chapter-34-p-6789131699: For sixty years Monte Carlo and MCMC sat in the optimization tradition's toolbox without crossing into the symbolic-AI mainstream. The Dartmouth program was about deduction; samplers were for physicists. Then, in 2006, a French researcher named Rémi Coulom, working on a Go-playing program called Crazy Stone, did something the symbolic tradition had given up on. He had no good heuristic for evaluating Go positions. Hand-built evaluation functions worked in chess because chess positions decompose into local patterns. Go positions don't decompose; the influence of a stone played in the upper-right corner can decide a fight in the lower-left forty moves later. The board's combinatorial space is roughly 1017010^{170}10170 legal positions, enormously larger than chess. No human had ever written down a heuristic that could see through it.
passages.chapter-34-p-1e6b821632: Coulom's idea, drawing on earlier work by Bruce Abramson and Bernd Brügmann, was: don't evaluate the position. Roll it out. From the current position, play games to the end with random moves. Do this many times. Average the outcomes. The statistic — the win rate from this position under random play — is a noisy but unbiased estimate of how good the position is. Branches with higher win rates get more rollouts; the search focuses where the statistics concentrate. Coulom called the method Monte Carlo Tree Search. He coined the term in a paper that year.
passages.chapter-34-p-9066d56c6f: Crazy Stone began beating professional Go players at handicaps that had previously been beyond computers. Within months Levente Kocsis and Csaba Szepesvári at SZTAKI in Budapest proposed UCT, an algorithm that balanced exploring uncertain branches against exploiting promising ones, and MCTS became the new state of the art. The wall that had stopped symbolic Go for thirty years yielded not to a cleverer heuristic but to a willingness to give up on heuristics and let random play do the searching.
passages.chapter-34-p-c3bbe339ec: Ten years later, at DeepMind, a researcher named Aja Huang led the engineering team on a system called AlphaGo. Huang had done his PhD under Coulom; the MCTS lineage was direct. What AlphaGo added was a pair of neural networks — one that proposed promising moves, one that evaluated positions — trained first on human games and then by self-play. MCTS was no longer rolling out random moves; the network proposed moves the way a strong player would, and the simulation tested whether the proposal worked. The two methods leaned on each other. The network's intuitions narrowed the search; the search corrected the network's mistakes; the results retrained the network. In March 2016, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol in Seoul. A year later, AlphaGo Zero learned the game from nothing but the rules and self-play, with MCTS as the teacher of the network and the network as the proposer to MCTS.
