passages.chapter-34-p-0389b9687b: When you imagine taking a different turn home and ask yourself whether it would be faster, you are not solving a routing problem. You are simulating the route — running a mental forward pass over the streets, sampling traffic, watching the simulation's clock against the one you remember. Children do it with marbles and ramps, chess players with positions, physicists with thought experiments. The brain, on the predictive-processing accounts the book will return to, is largely a forward-simulation engine, perpetually rolling out the next half-second of the world and adjusting its weights when reality disagrees. Friston and Clark would later argue that the cortex is doing something formally close to MCMC at every level — sampling hypotheses against incoming signal, settling into low-surprise equilibria.
passages.chapter-34-p-e89f05be4e: Pólya had written down the heuristics humans use to think. He had not written down the part where the mind runs a possible world to see what happens in it. The two methods — clever pruning and stochastic exploration — turned out to be the two ways past the combinatorial walls, and modern AI uses them fused. The neural network writes the heuristic; the simulation tests it; the result retrains the network. Ulam at Los Alamos with his deck of cards, Pólya at the ETH chalkboard, and Aja Huang at the Go board in Seoul were working on the same family of methods.

chapters.title: Chapter 35: The Real Wall

passages.chapter-35-p-1243e1b159: Gödel showed what formal systems can't prove. Turing showed what machines can't compute. The last two chapters showed two responses to a different kind of limit — Pólya's heuristics for pruning the search, the Monte Carlo method for sampling it. The limit itself has a name, and it is the third great boundary on what computation can do — arguably the one that matters most in practice.
passages.chapter-35-p-d27e1fb4f4: Some problems are computable but take longer than the age of the universe to solve.
passages.chapter-35-p-4992a36256: The distinction between what's computable and what's tractable is the distinction between theory and engineering — and it's the wall that actually constrains every machine you've ever used.
passages.chapter-35-p-ba4014b08d: In 1965, Jack Edmonds drew a line that computer science has been working with ever since. He distinguished "good" algorithms — those whose running time grows as a polynomial function of the input size — from "bad" ones, whose time grows exponentially. Double the input to a polynomial algorithm and the time might quadruple. Double the input to an exponential algorithm and the time might increase by a factor of a billion. In theory, both algorithms compute the answer. In practice, the exponential one is useless.
passages.chapter-35-p-e17297ff93: In 1971, Stephen Cook proved something remarkable: a specific problem called Boolean satisfiability — given a logical formula, is there an assignment of true and false that makes it true? — has a special property. If you can solve it efficiently, you can solve an enormous class of other problems efficiently too. It's as if thousands of seemingly unrelated problems are secretly the same problem wearing different clothes.
passages.chapter-35-p-6484bfba66: Richard Karp followed in 1972, showing that twenty-one important problems — scheduling, routing, packing, graph coloring — were all equivalent in this sense. Solve any one of them efficiently and you've solved them all. These problems are called NP-complete.
passages.chapter-35-p-23c11d4bf9: Nobody has ever found an efficient algorithm for any NP-complete problem. Nobody has ever proved that one can't exist. This is the P versus NP question — the most important open problem in computer science, carrying a million-dollar prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute. Most computer scientists believe P ≠ NP: that there are problems whose solutions can be quickly verified but never quickly found. But belief isn't proof, and the proof has resisted every approach for over fifty years.
passages.chapter-35-p-2700b2c90f: The actual wall that AI hits in practice is usually complexity, not computability. No one building a machine learning system worries about the halting problem. They worry about training time, about whether the loss landscape has tractable gradients or whether the optimization will get stuck in local minima for centuries of compute time, about the combinatorial explosion that happens when you try to reason about the real world — the number of possible chess positions, the number of possible protein folds, the number of possible ways a sentence could continue.
passages.chapter-35-p-1de6eed897: Gödel had shown that the dream was logically impossible; complexity theory showed that the achievable remainder was still astronomically hard.
passages.chapter-35-p-382a668439: Gradient descent works — when it works — because it sidesteps the combinatorial explosion. Instead of searching through all possible configurations (which would take exponential time), it follows the local gradient downhill (which takes polynomial time per step). It trades guarantee of finding the global optimum for tractability, accepting "good enough" instead of "best." This is the engineering bargain that makes modern AI possible — a bargain that the logical tradition, with its insistence on certainty and completeness, could never have accepted.
passages.chapter-35-p-06bbb16115: Suppose a puzzle has nnn independent binary choices. There are 2n2^n2n possible assignments. With 10 choices, that is 1,024. With 30, it is 1,073,741,824. With 60, it is about 1.15×10181.15\times10^{18}1.15×1018.
passages.chapter-35-p-4290a0c7f9: Imagine, purely for this calculation, a machine that examines a billion complete assignments each second with no overhead. Exhaustively checking 30 choices takes about a second. Checking 60 takes about 36.5 years. Doubling the number of choices did not double the work; it multiplied it by more than a billion.
passages.chapter-35-p-b6e2c749c7: Now separate finding from checking. Given one proposed satisfying assignment for a Boolean formula, we can evaluate the formula on it. That may be straightforward even when we do not know a fast general method for finding a satisfying assignment or establishing that none exists.
passages.chapter-35-p-4ea5fbbcad: This is a problem of computational complexity, distinct from undecidability. A brute-force search through finitely many assignments always terminates. The issue is how its resource requirements grow. NP-completeness is also not a proof that every instance is hard, nor a proof that no polynomial-time algorithm exists: the latter would require resolving P versus NP.
passages.chapter-35-p-191a3ac000: Structure changes the practical story. Solvers exploit constraints, learn from conflicts, and avoid visiting enormous regions of the search space. Some instances yield immediately; others resist. The exponential count warns us what naïve enumeration permits in the worst case. It does not report the running time of every competent solver on every real input.
passages.chapter-35-p-948d53a33e: When a system fails, ask which wall it met: an unrepresentable task, an undecidable universal demand, an expensive search, insufficient evidence, or a badly chosen objective. They can all look like “the machine could not do it,” while requiring very different responses.
passages.chapter-35-p-b60494fdef: The complexity wall also explains the AI winters — the periods of disillusionment that punctuate the field's history. Symbolic AI promised to reason about the world using logic. It worked for toy problems. Then it hit the complexity wall: the number of facts needed to represent common sense, the number of rules needed to handle exceptions to rules, the number of inferences needed to answer a simple question — all grew exponentially. The dream failed because logic, while correct, was intractable: the real world is NP-hard, and deduction doesn't scale.
passages.chapter-35-p-e0961cfd26: Neural networks found a different path. Gradient descent on a differentiable loss function navigates high-dimensional spaces that would be combinatorially impossible to search. What it finds isn't the logical answer but a statistical attractor — and for many practical purposes, that turns out to be enough.

chapters.title: Chapter 36: The Dartmouth Dream

passages.chapter-36-p-836399af5e: In the summer of 1956, a small group gathered at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. John McCarthy, a young mathematician at Dartmouth, had organized the workshop with a proposal that contained a sentence of breathtaking confidence:
passages.chapter-36-p-858758090d: "The study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it."
passages.chapter-36-p-0b9dce9ece: The proposal was co-authored by McCarthy, Marvin Minsky (a Harvard mathematician), Nathaniel Rochester (an IBM engineer), and Claude Shannon. The attendees included Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, who arrived with a working program — the Logic Theorist — that could prove theorems from Russell and Whitehead's Principia Mathematica.
passages.chapter-36-p-a396c0aae0: McCarthy coined the name "artificial intelligence" for the workshop — chosen, he later admitted, partly to distinguish the new field from Wiener's cybernetics. The name was a declaration of independence. Cybernetics was about feedback and control. Artificial intelligence was about thought and reasoning. The split was philosophical: cybernetics was bottom-up (adjust, minimize error, let behavior emerge), while AI would be top-down (represent knowledge, apply rules, deduce conclusions).
passages.chapter-36-p-69bbc9595f: The Dartmouth workshop produced no breakthroughs. But it defined a field, attracted funding, and installed a set of assumptions that would dominate for thirty years: intelligence is symbol manipulation, knowledge is a set of propositions, reasoning is logical inference. Build a big enough knowledge base, write enough rules, and intelligence will emerge. This was Leibniz's Calculemus! with transistors.
passages.chapter-36-p-1b2255d258: McCarthy went on to create LISP — Church's lambda calculus made into a programming language. Minsky built the MIT AI Lab into the most influential research group in the field. Newell and Simon pursued the "physical symbol system hypothesis": that a system capable of manipulating symbols has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action. The Logic Theorist they had brought to Dartmouth was the warm-up; the following year they would publish the General Problem Solver, an attempt to code Pólya's heuristics directly — means-ends analysis, working backward, problem decomposition — into a general-purpose machine.
passages.chapter-36-p-04fadf920d: The early successes were intoxicating: programs that proved theorems, played checkers, solved algebra word problems. SHRDLU, Terry Winograd's 1970 system, could understand natural language commands about a simulated world of colored blocks — "Pick up the red block that is on the blue block." It worked perfectly, within its tiny world.
passages.chapter-36-p-606867b8e5: The problem was that the tiny world was the trick. SHRDLU could reason about blocks because the blocks world had been completely specified. Every object, every property, every relation was defined in advance. Extend the approach to the real world and you'd need to specify everything — a task that turned out to be not just difficult but combinatorially impossible. This was the "frame problem" and the "common sense knowledge problem," and they were the first signs that the logical dream, translated into engineering, would hit the same walls it had hit in philosophy.

chapters.title: Chapter 37: Dreyfus's Heresy

passages.chapter-37-p-ce16684850: Hubert Dreyfus was a philosopher of phenomenology — a reader of Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty, a translator of Sense and Non-Sense, a man whose professional milieu was the question of what it means to have a body and a world. In 1962 he took a position at MIT, where Marvin Minsky and the Dartmouth founders were assembling what they believed would be, within a generation, a thinking machine. Dreyfus listened to them and came to the opposite conclusion. In 1965 he wrote it down.
passages.chapter-37-p-9a2631f0db: The document was a RAND Corporation paper called Alienation and Artificial Intelligence. It was widely circulated, more widely resented, and almost universally dismissed by the AI researchers it described. Dreyfus expanded it into What Computers Can't Do in 1972 and revised it again as What Computers Still Can't Do in 1992, the title doing its own work each time. His central claim drew straight from the European tradition his American colleagues had never read. Heidegger had argued that human understanding is grounded in being-in-the-world — a tacit, embodied, pre-theoretical familiarity with how things hang together that no explicit set of rules could ever capture. Merleau-Ponty had developed the phenomenology of skilled action: a chess master sees the position, a driver feels the road, a doctor recognizes the sick child without consulting a checklist. The skill lives in the body's history of engagement, not in a database the body queries.
passages.chapter-37-p-dc6964ce1c: Symbolic AI, Dreyfus argued, was trying to reconstruct that familiarity by listing it. The Newell-Simon physical-symbol-system hypothesis assumed that all of human competence could in principle be written down as facts and rules. Dreyfus thought this was a category mistake. The background know-how that lets you understand a sentence, navigate a room, or recognize that a triangle with sides 5, 3, 8 is degenerate is not a finite list of propositions; it is a horizon of involvement that the propositional mode presupposes rather than produces. Try to enumerate it and you encounter what AI researchers would later call the frame problem, the common-sense problem, the qualification problem — each one a different face of the same wall.
passages.chapter-37-p-6e27b0eb57: The reception was vicious. Seymour Papert wrote a rebuttal titled The Artificial Intelligence of Hubert L. Dreyfus: A Budget of Fallacies. MIT denied him a tenured appointment; he eventually left for Berkeley. The most public humiliation came at the chessboard. Dreyfus, an amateur player, had used chess as one of his standing examples — surely, he said, no programmer would build a chess machine that played well, because chess competence is a kind of recognitional skill that resists formalization. In 1967, Richard Greenblatt's MIT program MacHack VI played him in a tournament game and won. The AI Lab posted the score sheet. Seymour Papert's RAND review reprinted it.
passages.chapter-37-p-b514ba4128: Dreyfus did not pretend the loss had not happened. The second edition of What Computers Can't Do contained a corrected passage and an extended discussion of what MacHack's victory did and did not show. A program can play strong chess by searching deeper than a human can. The fact that it does so without anything resembling chess understanding was, he insisted, exactly his point: brute search is not a model of human competence, it is a way of getting the same outputs by a different route. He kept publishing.
passages.chapter-37-p-9aefc0b73e: Forty years later, every wall Dreyfus had named had become a research problem. The frame problem became the brittleness of expert systems. The qualification problem became the AI winters Edward Feigenbaum's students described in defeated retrospectives. Common-sense reasoning consumed Doug Lenat's Cyc project for three decades and produced no general intelligence. By the time the field gave up on the symbolic program and turned to gradient descent on neural networks, Dreyfus had been right about the symbolic approach for so long that even his old opponents were quoting him. Mind Over Machine (1986), written with his brother Stuart Dreyfus — an operations researcher whose own work on dynamic programming had shaped early reinforcement learning — laid out a five-stage model of skill acquisition from novice to expert that anticipated, in plain language, what the connectionists were about to formalize in math.
passages.chapter-37-p-d7744d8ea7: Deep learning sidestepped him rather than refuting him. The neural-network approach gave up on explicit symbolic representation entirely and learned distributed patterns from data, which is to say it built systems whose competence is recognitional and whose knowledge is tacit — closer in shape to the phenomenology Dreyfus had been defending than to the GOFAI he had been criticizing. The walls he had identified are still there: an LLM has no body, no world, no horizon of involvement, and its failures cluster precisely where embodied background know-how is what the task requires.
passages.chapter-37-p-05a44e9ddc: Dreyfus died in 2017, the year Attention Is All You Need was published.

chapters.title: Chapter 38: The Winters

passages.chapter-38-p-a77a413234: The first wave — symbolic AI, expert systems — peaked in the early 1980s. Japan launched the Fifth Generation Computer Project, aiming to build machines that reasoned in Prolog. Corporations spent billions on expert systems: programs that encoded human expertise as if-then rules. The promise: capture what doctors know, what engineers know, what geologists know, and deploy it at scale.
passages.chapter-38-p-42bd4ae15b: The systems worked in narrow domains. MYCIN diagnosed bacterial infections. DENDRAL identified molecular structures. R1 configured computer orders for Digital Equipment Corporation. But they were brittle. Step outside the domain and they collapsed. They couldn't learn, couldn't handle ambiguity, couldn't deal with the fact that real-world expertise is largely tacit — encoded in practice, not in propositions. The frame problem, the common sense problem, the qualification problem — every issue the philosophers had identified showed up in engineering.
passages.chapter-38-p-9c3adc3e62: Funding dried up. The Fifth Generation Project quietly failed. The expert systems market collapsed. The first AI winter had arrived by the late 1980s.
passages.chapter-38-p-957d393a5b: The symbolic-AI program of the 1970s and 1980s was Robert Moses's planning vision applied to cognition: top-down rules, comprehensive ontologies, knowledge bases authored by experts and validated by committees, a confident assumption that intelligent behaviour could be specified in advance by people who knew enough. What eventually replaced it was closer to Jane Jacobs's unplanned-city epistemology — bottom-up learning from data, structure that emerged from interaction rather than being decreed, no central designer claiming to know what the system should look like. The deep-learning wave that followed was a different theory of where knowledge comes from, not merely a better algorithm for representing it.
passages.chapter-38-p-e3749aa6de: Meanwhile, in the other tradition — the connectionist, bottom-up, optimization tradition — neural networks had been struggling. Rosenblatt's perceptron, introduced in 1958, could learn simple classifications by adjusting weights to minimize error. It was gradient descent on a simple loss surface, and it worked. The New York Times reported that the Navy had built a machine that could "walk, talk, see, write, reproduce itself, and be conscious of its existence."
passages.chapter-38-p-accd8bc177: Then Minsky and Papert published Perceptrons in 1969. Their book proved, rigorously, that single-layer perceptrons couldn't learn certain simple functions — specifically, XOR. The proof was correct. The implication they drew — that multilayer networks were unlikely to overcome these limitations — was wrong. But the damage was catastrophic. Funding for neural network research evaporated for over a decade. One correct theorem about one architecture, extrapolated into a death sentence for the entire approach. The field couldn't tell the difference between a local limitation and a fundamental one.
passages.chapter-38-p-89d2edb533: The second wave came with backpropagation. The idea — propagate errors backward through a multilayer network and adjust weights by gradient descent — had been discovered independently by Paul Werbos (1974), David Parker (1985), and Yann LeCun (early 1980s), and popularized by Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams in 1986. It showed that multilayer networks could learn XOR and far more. The limitation Minsky and Papert had identified was real but narrow.
passages.chapter-38-p-1b9264447a: But computing power was insufficient. Data was scarce. Neural networks worked on toy problems and failed to scale. A second winter descended through the 1990s, during which statistical methods — support vector machines, random forests, Bayesian approaches — dominated machine learning without the grand claims of either symbolic AI or neural networks.
passages.chapter-38-p-85f677e565: This quiet interregnum deserves a moment's attention, because the Bayesian methods that flourished in the 1990s were the direct descendants of Ramsey's 1926 insight. Start with degrees of belief. Observe data. Update by Bayes's rule. The prior washes out as evidence accumulates. The Bayesian machine learning community — David MacKay, Radford Neal, Michael Jordan — built models that combined structured assumptions with probabilistic learning, exactly the fusion Ramsey had formalized. They didn't scale. They needed too much computation per inference. But they were the most principled learners anyone had built, and their framework — priors, likelihoods, posteriors — would quietly infiltrate the deep learning revolution when it came. Variational autoencoders, Bayesian neural networks, uncertainty estimation: the optimization tradition kept rediscovering that it needed probability, just as Ramsey had shown it would.
passages.chapter-38-p-497e44da51: The third wave — deep learning — arrived around 2012 with AlexNet, and it has not yet crested. What changed was compute (GPUs), data (the internet), and architectural innovations (dropout, batch normalization, residual connections, attention). The optimization tradition had finally found its moment: enough data to define the loss landscape, enough compute to descend the gradients, enough architectural tricks to navigate the complexity.
passages.chapter-38-p-b815a88aa8: Then, in 2017, a team at Google published a paper with an unusually direct title: "Attention Is All You Need." The transformer architecture replaced the sequential processing of earlier networks with something conceptually simpler and far more powerful: attention. Each element of the input can "look at" every other element and learn how much each one matters. A word at the end of a sentence can attend directly to a word at the beginning, without the signal degrading through a chain of intermediate steps. This solved long-range dependencies — the problem that had plagued language models for years — and it was massively parallelizable, which meant it could exploit GPU hardware in a way sequential models couldn't.
passages.chapter-38-p-7fa8a130dc: GPT — the Generative Pre-trained Transformer — was the consequence. Take the transformer architecture, train it on next-token prediction (given all the words so far, predict the next one), and scale it up. The training objective is the cross-entropy loss Shannon's information theory defined: minimize the difference between the model's predicted probability distribution and the actual distribution of next tokens. The learning process is gradient descent — Cauchy's 1847 method, applied to billions of parameters — running on Boolean circuits that are Boole's algebra implemented in Shannon's silicon. The representations that emerge are Saussurean: meaning from differences, positions in a vector space defined by relations to other positions. And the system lacks grounding — Wittgenstein's diagnosis, arriving on schedule.
passages.chapter-38-p-eeb4fa49a1: Every thread in this book converges in the transformer. The machine that logic built, running an optimization process that isn't logic, trained on an information-theoretic objective, producing representations that confirm a structural linguist's century-old theory, and hitting the walls that philosophers mapped decades before anyone wrote the first line of code.
passages.chapter-38-p-8b0ccc6a21: Deep learning doesn't try to encode knowledge as rules or specify the world in advance. It follows the gradient downhill through a loss landscape shaped by data, and lets the representations emerge. The failure of the logical approach didn't kill AI; it redirected the field toward the optimization tradition, which had been running, underappreciated, since Cauchy.
passages.chapter-38-p-33efb47a9a: But the transformer didn't arrive in a vacuum. To understand how "scale is all you need" became a research program and a funding thesis, you need the institutions that turned the optimization tradition from a scientific insight into an industrial project.
passages.chapter-38-p-eb451ffce7: The story begins with a dataset. In 2009, Fei-Fei Li, a computer science professor at Stanford, launched ImageNet — a database of over 14 million hand-labeled images organized into more than 20,000 categories. The annual ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, starting in 2010, asked teams to build systems that could classify images into a thousand categories. For two years, progress was incremental — accuracy improvements of a few percentage points per year, using hand-engineered features and traditional machine learning methods.
passages.chapter-38-p-55a09dafe6: Then, in 2012, Hinton's team entered AlexNet. The error rate didn't improve by a few points. It dropped by nearly half — from 26% to 16%. The result didn't just win the competition. It ended it as a meaningful contest. Within two years, deep neural networks dominated every entry, and the error rate continued to fall until it surpassed human performance. ImageNet became the proof point that made the scaling thesis feel inevitable: this architecture, with more data and more compute, produced gains that no amount of hand-engineering could match.
passages.chapter-38-p-f41a9b5c66: ImageNet also created a culture. The competition format — shared benchmarks, public leaderboards, reproducible results — turned AI research from a field of competing paradigms into something closer to a sport. You could measure progress. You could compare approaches. And the scorecard pointed relentlessly in one direction: bigger models, more data, more compute.
passages.chapter-38-p-0606b3c7a3: Two institutions crystallized around this moment. In 2010, Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, and Mustafa Suleyman founded DeepMind in London. Hassabis was a chess prodigy turned neuroscientist turned game designer — an unusual combination that reflected DeepMind's unusual ambition. Legg had written a PhD thesis on the mathematical definition of machine intelligence and believed deeply that general intelligence was a solvable engineering problem. Their stated mission was to "solve intelligence, and then use that to solve everything else." Google acquired DeepMind in 2014 for approximately $500 million. In 2016, their system AlphaGo defeated Lee Sedol, the world champion at Go — a game that the AI community had considered decades away from being solved. The optimization tradition had conquered a domain that was supposed to require human intuition.
passages.chapter-38-p-35ee216a91: In 2015, OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit research lab by Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and others, with the mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ilya Sutskever — Hinton's former student, co-creator of AlexNet — became chief scientist. Sutskever brought with him a conviction that would define OpenAI's research direction: that scaling neural networks was the primary path to general intelligence. The route wasn't better algorithms or new architectures; it was scale. Make the models bigger, give them more data, increase the compute, and the intelligence would emerge.
passages.chapter-38-p-667e4373ae: This conviction had theoretical grounding before it had a name. In 2018, Google released BERT — Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Where GPT read text left to right, predicting the next word, BERT read in both directions simultaneously, learning to fill in missing words from their full context. BERT was trained on the entirety of English Wikipedia and a large book corpus, and it immediately set new records on eleven natural language processing benchmarks. The result was striking not for the architecture — which was the same transformer — but for what the scaling revealed. A single pre-trained model, fine-tuned with minimal additional data, could outperform years of task-specific engineering across wildly different language tasks. The representations learned from sheer volume of text were transferable in ways no one had fully anticipated.
passages.chapter-38-p-98cc01bf46: GPT-2 followed in 2019, with 1.5 billion parameters. OpenAI initially declined to release the full model, citing concerns about misuse — the first time a lab had withheld an AI system on safety grounds, and a decision that generated both praise and skepticism. GPT-3, released in 2020, had 175 billion parameters — over a hundred times larger. It could write essays, generate code, translate languages, and answer questions with a fluency that shocked even its creators. The jump from GPT-2 to GPT-3 wasn't just bigger. It was qualitatively different. Capabilities appeared that no one had explicitly trained for — what researchers would later call "emergent abilities." The system wasn't programmed to do arithmetic or write poetry. It learned to do both, roughly, as side effects of learning to predict the next word at sufficient scale.
passages.chapter-38-p-e629af9e45: Then, in January 2020, a paper gave the scaling thesis its mathematical backbone. Jared Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI published "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." The paper demonstrated that language model performance follows precise power laws: the loss decreases predictably as you increase model size, dataset size, or compute. The relationship held across seven orders of magnitude. Architectural details — network width, depth, specific design choices — had minimal effect compared to raw scale. The paper's conclusion was remarkable in its simplicity and its ambition: performance is a smooth, predictable function of how much you spend. If you want a better model, spend more. The curve told you exactly how much.
passages.chapter-38-p-f08d10a952: This was the moment the optimization tradition acquired the confidence of the logical tradition. Kaplan's scaling laws were presented, and received, as empirical regularities with the force of natural law. "Scale is all you need" wasn't just a slogan. It was a research program backed by what looked like mathematical proof. The parallel to physics was explicit: power laws, universal exponents, predictions that held across orders of magnitude.
passages.chapter-38-p-54b43d6ebe: Sutskever was the most prominent and articulate champion of this thesis. He argued that the scaling laws pointed toward a specific conclusion: that general intelligence would emerge from next-token prediction at sufficient scale — not because anyone had designed intelligence or because the architecture encoded reasoning, but because the optimization process, running long enough on enough data, would discover internal representations that amounted to understanding. The bet was enormous, and Sutskever made it with a conviction that struck observers as either visionary or religious — a distinction that depended on whether you believed the scaling laws would hold indefinitely.
passages.chapter-38-p-f7a5fdf50f: OpenAI bet its existence on this conviction. GPT-4, released in 2023, was trained on a reported 25,000 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. The cost of a single training run was estimated in the tens of millions of dollars. DeepMind, backed by Google's resources, pursued a parallel track, developing Gemini to compete with GPT-4. Anthropic, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers Dario and Daniela Amodei, built Claude on similar foundations. The race to scale consumed hundreds of billions of dollars in infrastructure investment. Data centers proliferated. Chip manufacturers couldn't meet demand. The compute used to train a leading model in 2023 was ten billion times higher than it had been in 2010.
passages.chapter-38-p-75e4717a5c: The optimization tradition had never in its history been the recipient of this kind of capital. Gauss minimized errors with pen and paper. Cauchy followed gradients in thought experiments. Boltzmann worked out statistical mechanics with chalk. Now their intellectual descendants were building systems that required the electrical output of small cities.
passages.chapter-38-p-639cac1bbe: The optimization thread has been surfacing throughout this book — Gauss minimizing errors, Cauchy following gradients, Boltzmann finding equilibria, Rosenblatt adjusting weights, the repeated rediscovery of backpropagation. Each chapter added a strand.
passages.chapter-38-p-b9df4ef5d7: Start with the deepest rediscovery: Charles Darwin described the same process in biology. Natural selection is optimization on a fitness landscape. Organisms vary randomly. The environment selects. Over generations, the population moves downhill on the loss surface — "loss" being, in this case, failure to reproduce. Darwin didn't have the mathematics. But the structure is identical: variation, evaluation against a function (fitness), adjustment in the direction of better performance.
passages.chapter-38-p-1ab2d893d8: Hopfield networks in 1982 made the physics connection explicit: neural networks have energy functions, and the network dynamics minimize that energy. A Hopfield network settling into a stored pattern is a physical system finding its energy minimum — Boltzmann's statistical mechanics, implemented in silicon. Hinton and Sejnowski named their 1985 creation the Boltzmann machine precisely because it used stochastic dynamics inspired by statistical physics to find low-energy configurations.
passages.chapter-38-p-2497f1b591: Kirkpatrick's simulated annealing in 1983 borrowed the metaphor from metallurgy: heat a metal, then cool it slowly. The atoms explore the energy landscape while hot, then settle into a low-energy crystalline structure as they cool. Do the same with a computational search: allow random jumps early (exploration), then gradually reduce randomness (exploitation). The metal finds good configurations not by logic but by thermodynamics.
passages.chapter-38-p-c731f81870: Each rediscovery was independent, coming from a different field with its own vocabulary: Cauchy called it "steepest descent," Boltzmann "thermal equilibrium," Darwin "natural selection," Rosenblatt "learning," Werbos "backpropagation," Hopfield "energy minimization."
passages.chapter-38-p-b87197ac23: When Church, Turing, and Post independently defined computability, the convergence suggested that computability was a natural category — a discovery, not an invention. The convergence around gradient descent is far broader — spanning two centuries, five fields, and a dozen independent discoverers. Optimization by iterative error reduction is a structural constraint on how complex systems learn, adapt, and find order.
passages.chapter-38-p-f553ff77be: Logic was one way to make machines useful; optimization was another. The second tradition was never absent — it was running alongside the first, waiting for the hardware to catch up. The optimization tradition's century-long detour through statistical mechanics and biology is what now drives the systems the symbolic program failed to build.
passages.chapter-38-p-f48ea1d3b8: The computer that logic built is running a process that logic cannot explain.

chapters.title: Chapter 39: The Science of Mind

passages.chapter-40-p-c406996819: The same war was fought inside the study of the mind itself. And the results map the current AI landscape more precisely than any philosophical argument alone.
passages.chapter-40-p-34d44a9e4b: In the 1950s and 1960s, cognitive science was born — and it was born firmly on the logic thread's side. Noam Chomsky's 1959 review of B.F. Skinner's Verbal Behavior was the founding strike. Behaviorism — the idea that the mind is a blank slate shaped by association and reinforcement, stimulus and response — had dominated psychology for decades. Chomsky demolished it in thirty pages. Language can't be learned by association alone. Children produce sentences they've never heard. They master grammatical rules no one taught them. They converge on the same deep structure from wildly different inputs. The only explanation: the mind has innate structure — not a blank slate but a machine with a program.
passages.chapter-40-p-9ad2935f6a: This was Frege's dream translated into psychology. The mind computes, manipulating symbols according to rules, with a formal structure that determines what it can and cannot produce. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon took the analogy literally: they built the Logic Theorist (1956) and the General Problem Solver, programs that solved problems by searching through symbolic representations the way a mathematician searches through proofs. Their "physical symbol system hypothesis" was the logic thread's boldest claim about the mind: a physical system has the necessary and sufficient means for intelligent action if and only if it can manipulate symbols.
passages.chapter-40-p-17ad957d23: Jerry Fodor pushed it further. In The Language of Thought (1975), he argued that thinking just is computation over mental representations that have language-like structure. Thoughts combine like sentences: you understand "the dog bit the cat" and automatically understand "the cat bit the dog" because your mental representations are compositional — built from parts that can be recombined. This property, systematicity, is what makes thought productive. You can think an infinite number of thoughts from a finite vocabulary of concepts, the same way you can produce infinite sentences from a finite grammar.
passages.chapter-40-p-42859becb9: For two decades, this was cognitive science: the mind was a computer, cognition was symbol manipulation, and the research program was to reverse-engineer the software.
passages.chapter-40-p-381f10b943: Then the optimization thread broke through.
passages.chapter-40-p-88cea98279: In 1986, James McClelland and David Rumelhart published two volumes under the title Parallel Distributed Processing. The books reignited a tradition that Minsky and Papert had nearly killed. The core idea: cognition isn't symbol manipulation but pattern activation across networks of simple units — units that look like neurons, connected by weights that look like synapses, learning by adjusting those weights to reduce error. No rules, no symbols, no program — just a loss function and a gradient.
passages.chapter-40-p-abfe5e15cb: The PDP group showed that these networks could learn past tenses of English verbs, recognize handwritten digits, and acquire concepts — all without being programmed with rules. The network that learned to produce "went" from "go" didn't store a rule that said "go → went (irregular)." It developed a pattern of connection strengths that produced the right output for the right input. The knowledge was in the connections, distributed across the entire network.
passages.chapter-40-p-a9be7abbdb: This was Hebb's 1949 principle — neurons that fire together wire together — scaled up with Cauchy's gradient descent.
passages.chapter-40-p-d1095b775d: Fodor and Zenon Pylyshyn fired back immediately. Their 1988 paper, "Connectionism and Cognitive Architecture," is the logic thread's strongest counterattack, and it has never been fully answered.
passages.chapter-40-p-7c2739c923: The argument: connectionist networks can't explain systematicity. If you understand "John loves Mary," you automatically understand "Mary loves John." This isn't something you learn separately. It follows from the compositional structure of your representations — you have a concept for "John," a concept for "Mary," a concept for "loves," and a way of combining them that generates both sentences and both meanings. A network that learns "John loves Mary" as a pattern of activation has no guarantee that it can produce the reversed form. It would have to learn each combination independently. The combinatorial explosion would be infinite.
passages.chapter-40-p-121ad8d82a: Fodor wasn't saying networks couldn't do useful things. He was saying they couldn't be the format of thought. The mind needs compositional, language-like structure at some level of description. Pure pattern matching — no matter how sophisticated — can't produce the systematicity that is the most basic feature of human cognition.
passages.chapter-40-p-b893033f5d: This is the logic thread saying to the optimization thread: you can approximate my outputs, but you can't replicate my structure. You can learn to produce "Mary loves John" if it's in your training data, but you don't understand why the words can be rearranged or what the rearrangement means. Your competence is statistical; mine is structural.
passages.chapter-40-p-881e2d5ba2: That objection — unanswered in 1988 — is the most precise description of what large language models do and don't do that anyone has ever written.
passages.chapter-40-p-044da21ace: Fodor wasn't making a prediction about technology. He was identifying a structural constraint: any system whose knowledge is distributed across connection weights, rather than composed from discrete symbols, will approximate compositional behavior without possessing compositional structure. It will produce "Mary loves John" when the training data contains that pattern, and fail unpredictably when the pattern is absent — not because it's insufficiently trained, but because the format of its knowledge doesn't support the operation. That gap between approximation and structure is where every surprising LLM failure lives. The hallucinations, the confident nonsense, the inability to reliably negate or reverse — all are symptoms of distributed representations lacking compositional machinery.
passages.chapter-40-p-222f6fa38d: While the symbolists and connectionists fought about architecture, a third group was questioning the entire debate's premises.
passages.chapter-40-p-8b3d4d1c2e: James Gibson, an American psychologist who had spent World War II studying how pilots perceive depth, proposed something radical in The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979). Perception isn't building internal models and running inference; it's directly detecting affordances — action possibilities in the environment. You don't compute that a chair is sittable by constructing a mental representation and matching it against a concept. You perceive the sit-ability directly, because your body and the chair are coupled in a way that makes the affordance available.
passages.chapter-40-p-2aaf00b831: This was Heidegger's "ready-to-hand" translated into experimental psychology. The hammer isn't primarily an object with properties you represent and reason about. It's something you use. Understanding what a hammer is means knowing how to hammer. That knowledge lives in the coupling between body and world, not in a symbol in your head.
passages.chapter-40-p-8538bdd8dc: Rodney Brooks, building robots at MIT in the late 1980s, turned this into engineering. His paper "Intelligence Without Representation" (1991) described robots that had no internal world model. No symbols, no planning, no central processor maintaining a map of the environment. Instead, layers of behavior coupled directly to sensors: detect obstacle, turn; see light, approach; feel contact, retreat. These robots navigated real-world environments better than the symbolic AI robots that maintained elaborate internal representations. The world was its own best model. You didn't need to represent it if you were embedded in it.
passages.chapter-40-p-00269da525: Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, and Eleanor Rosch synthesized this into a philosophical program. The Embodied Mind (1991) argued that cognition isn't abstract computation running on a brain that happens to be housed in a body. Cognition is enacted through the body's engagement with the world. The mind isn't in the head; it's in the loop — the continuous cycle of perception, action, and adjustment that constitutes a living organism's history of coupling with its environment.
passages.chapter-40-p-c6fd852924: Andy Clark took it further. Being There (1997) proposed that the mind extends beyond the skull. A pen and paper aren't just tools you use to think; they're part of the cognitive system. An engineer with a calculator thinks differently, not just faster, than an engineer without one. Cognition is distributed across brain, body, and environment.
passages.chapter-40-p-176cb34fab: This reframes everything the book has been building toward. When you wrap an LLM in external checks — test suites, verification layers, human review — you aren't compensating for a deficit; you're building the cognitive system that the model alone can never be. The scaffold isn't an add-on but a necessary component of any system that claims to know things. We've always needed them — institutions, peer review, the scientific method. The LLM makes the need visible because the gap between the model and the scaffold is so stark.
passages.chapter-40-p-74c571d4a6: There was a deeper thread running beneath all of these debates, and it connected back to a mind that had been dead for sixty years.
passages.chapter-40-p-9b08dd09ba: Ramsey showed in 1926 that rational belief must obey probability — that updating confidence in light of evidence isn't just one way of learning but the only coherent way. That insight sat in philosophy for decades while the cognitive revolution built its symbolic architecture. Then, in the late 1990s and 2000s, a group of researchers at MIT — Joshua Tenenbaum, Thomas Griffiths, Noah Goodman — asked a question that neither the symbolists nor the connectionists had properly formulated: how do humans learn so much from so little?
passages.chapter-40-p-e8c0b7bfbd: A child sees three or four examples of dogs and grasps the concept — not just memorizing the examples but generalizing. A new animal that looks somewhat dog-like is correctly categorized; a cat that superficially resembles the examples is correctly excluded. A statistical learner trained on four examples would be hopelessly underconstrained. The data doesn't determine the concept; something else does.
passages.chapter-40-p-7f10f9abf4: The answer, Tenenbaum argued, is structured Bayesian inference. The child isn't learning from the examples alone. The child brings priors — structured expectations about how the world works. Objects belong to kinds. Kinds have typical features. Features cluster in reliable ways. Given those structural priors, even a few examples are enough to massively update the posterior. The math is Ramsey's: start with degrees of belief, observe evidence, update by Bayes's rule. But the priors aren't flat. They encode the deep structure of the world — causality, object permanence, spatial reasoning, folk physics, folk psychology. The child's head isn't empty before the examples arrive; it's loaded with a generative model of how dogs get produced — what process in the world gives rise to the data the child observes.
passages.chapter-40-p-05650389de: This is the logic and optimization threads fused inside a single theory of mind. The generative model has compositional, language-like structure — Fodor's demand. The learning happens through probabilistic inference — the optimization tradition's method. Goodman built a programming language (Church, later WebPPL) for expressing cognitive models as probabilistic programs: symbolic structures that generate data probabilistically, inverted by Bayesian inference to recover the structure from the data.
passages.chapter-40-p-066cd6f19b: The punchline for AI: Bayesian cognitive science says human learning is inference over structured causal models. You don't just learn that fire is hot from statistical co-occurrence. You build a causal model — fire causes heat — that lets you predict, intervene, and reason counterfactually. "If I hadn't touched it, I wouldn't have burned." That counterfactual requires a model of the causal process, not a correlation table.
passages.chapter-40-p-5f634669c4: LLMs have no causal models, only correlations over text. They can produce the sentence "fire causes heat," but they cannot reason about what would happen if the fire weren't there.
passages.chapter-40-p-26295bea79: This is where a different line of research — decades old, from a completely different discipline — provides the diagnostic framework that matters most for understanding what language models are.
passages.chapter-40-p-10bbf2ee63: In the 1970s, the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky began documenting something that should have been impossible: systematic, predictable irrationality in human reasoning. Not random errors or stupidity, but patterned failures — failures that revealed the structure underneath.
passages.chapter-40-p-0aa1b29ea1: Availability bias: people judge probability by how easily examples come to mind, not by actual frequency. A plane crash makes flying feel dangerous; driving feels safe because car accidents don't make the news. Anchoring: a random number on a spinning wheel influences people's estimates of African countries in the UN, even when they know the number is random. Representativeness: people judge probability by resemblance rather than base rates — a quiet, bookish person "must be" a librarian rather than a salesman, even though there are vastly more salesmen.
passages.chapter-40-p-de2ca16688: Each failure had the same signature: fast, associative, pattern-matching cognition producing confident answers that systematic reasoning would have caught. Kahneman formalized this as the dual-process model in Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), drawing on forty years of work. System 1 is fast, automatic, associative — it recognizes faces, completes phrases, matches patterns. System 2 is slow, deliberate, effortful — it checks arithmetic, follows logical arguments, weighs evidence. Both are necessary. Neither is sufficient alone. And the failures of human reasoning are precisely the failures of System 1 operating without System 2's oversight.
passages.chapter-40-p-3100b071b1: This matters for AI because it's the most precise diagnostic we have. LLMs are System 1 at a scale no human brain can match — fast, associative, pattern-matching, running across the entire statistical landscape of human language. What they lack is System 2 — slow, deliberate, structured reasoning that builds and manipulates models of the world.
passages.chapter-40-p-585aede228: An LLM failing is System 1 failing: fluent, confident, and wrong. The review model that surfaced polished nonsense over messy truth, the moderation system that couldn't distinguish anger from abuse — pattern matching at scale, without the structured model that would catch the error.
passages.chapter-40-p-2de1c26fff: The final convergence came from neuroscience.
passages.chapter-40-p-01d8cf451f: Hermann von Helmholtz — a contemporary of Boltzmann, already in this book's orbit — proposed in the 1860s that perception is "unconscious inference." The brain doesn't passively receive sensory data. It generates predictions about what it expects to see, then updates when the predictions fail. You perceive what your brain predicts, corrected by the error between prediction and reality.
passages.chapter-40-p-90e92c24a5: A century and a half later, Karl Friston formalized this as the free energy principle: the brain is a prediction engine that minimizes surprise — the gap between what it expects and what it encounters. Perception, action, learning — all aspects of the same process of reducing error and adjusting the model. Andy Clark, in Surfing Uncertainty (2015), made the case that this is the organizing principle of the entire brain: a cascading hierarchy of predictions flowing downward, error signals flowing upward, the whole system continuously tuning itself against reality.
passages.chapter-40-p-ecbdd2601f: This is gradient descent running on neurons — Cauchy's 1847 method implemented in biological tissue, and Ramsey's rational belief revision running continuously and automatically. Helmholtz, who proposed it, was Boltzmann's teacher.
passages.chapter-40-p-c799ce3364: But — and this is where it matters for everything that follows — the brain's prediction engine is grounded in a body that moves through a physical world. The error signal comes from reality. When your brain predicts the cup is on the left and your hand reaches left and finds nothing, the prediction error is generated by the physics of the world, not by the statistics of a text corpus. The updating is real, the checking is real, the world pushes back.
passages.chapter-40-p-2bc3e48e59: An LLM is a prediction engine without the world. Its error signal during training is the gap between its predicted next token and the actual next token in a text. Same optimization principle, same gradient descent — but fundamentally different grounding. Ramsey's bridge between the logic and optimization threads showed what rational belief requires — evidence that makes contact with the world. The LLM architecture shows what happens when you run the optimization without the contact.
passages.chapter-40-p-59a65fbe7a: Three lines of evidence. Philosophy said understanding requires embodied participation in forms of life. Cognitive science spent fifty years establishing that cognition is enacted through body-environment coupling, structured by causal models, checked against reality. And the production systems that run on text alone — systems I've built, deployed, and watched fail — fail in exactly the ways both traditions predicted.

chapters.title: Chapter 40: Your Wall

passages.chapter-41-p-ddc84ee6ec: When was the last time you built a system that did something you couldn't explain? I don't mean a bug — bugs are explicable in principle, even when the root cause takes a week to find. I mean the other thing. The output that survives every sanity check you can think of and still leaves you with a feeling, sitting in front of the screen, that the system is succeeding for reasons that have nothing to do with the reason you built it to succeed.
passages.chapter-41-p-47bd4eaee2: If you work with machine-learned systems you have probably been in that meeting. The model's accuracy on the held-out set is good. The calibration plot is reasonable. The reviewer asks one question — how is it doing this for inputs from a population that wasn't in training? — and the answer is a confidence score on a class the model has never been graded against, because nobody on the team thought to grade it, because nobody on the team realized the class existed until the model started predicting it. The confusion matrix has a column you don't have a label for. The numbers in that column are large.
passages.chapter-41-p-44fb840a2b: Or maybe you don't work with ML. Maybe you write the kind of software where a heuristic has been doing fine for three years and then one Tuesday it fails on a case that, when you look at it carefully, is not the kind of case the heuristic was ever supposed to handle — and your colleague's instinct is to add a special case, and your instinct is something else, something harder to name, that the special case is a symptom of a problem in how you defined the inputs in the first place. The fix in the ticket and the fix in your head are not the same fix.
passages.chapter-41-p-c389bca373: Or maybe you're a researcher. The result is robust to the seven things you checked it against. It survived two reviewers. It is the cleanest experimental signal you have produced this year. You cannot stop reading the methods section. Something in the design is off-axis from what the result claims, and the gap is not where any of the standard objections live.
passages.chapter-41-p-4621ef6717: The thing you are looking at is not a bug. It is a place where the framework you are using to interpret your own system has run out of grip.
passages.chapter-41-p-c0f4ea8454: The philosophers we followed did not describe one identical wall. Hume asked about the warrant for generalization, Wittgenstein about use, and Gödel about proof within formal systems meeting particular conditions. Bringing them together helps if it distinguishes the problem we face. Calling everything a “limit” can itself become a way of missing the differences.
passages.chapter-41-p-0c6b8cf435: Hold a real moment of your own in mind. What was asked of the system? What did you actually measure? If the two differ, what evidence could expose the gap? Part IV will return from these questions to philosophy. Not every error is a structural limit, and not every limit establishes impossibility. Sometimes the program needs repair; sometimes the question does.
passages.chapter-41-p-54af04691a: What would it take to recognize, in advance, the shape of a problem your tools are not built to solve? What would change about the meeting if the question on the table were where is the grounding signal coming from, rather than what is the test accuracy?
passages.chapter-41-p-b1fe798592: From Turing’s tape we reached a machine that writes an answer and can sometimes use a tool to check it. History has not supplied a final guarantee. It has supplied ways to distinguish what we requested from what we obtained. Now we return to the present. Keep your own example with you; the story has reached the decision you will make.
